positioning: Everyday citizen-scale problems that students can investigate and potentially solve; the card title and all six front scenes identify the problem, not a selected product or service.
funding_policy: Amounts are optional cash ceilings for a 7–14 day first experiment, scaled to the problem, not grants required to begin or full launch costs. Students should use existing tools and willing partners, pay for any extra work, test with real users, and name what evidence would justify a larger seed or angel investment later.
agency_goal: Students should leave each card seeing a nearby problem they can investigate and a first action they can afford this week. They may spend less than the ceiling or nothing at all.
card_authoring_rule: The visible front shows causes, constraints, current workarounds, and consequences. The reverse questions build toward an open proposal; no one solution is presented as the answer.
visual_policy: Six distinct action scenes, labels over matching pictures, Bangladesh/Rajshahi material context. Depicted women wear three-pieces with ornas or burkas. No legible sensitive details in artwork.

cards.title: SPOILED TIFFIN
cards.focus: Food packed in the morning may become unsafe or unappetizing before lunch in Rajshahi's summer heat.

tiles.label: Morning Packing
tiles.scene: A Bangladeshi parent packs rice and vegetable curry into a reusable steel tiffin box before a Rajshahi student leaves home.

tiles.label: Sunny Commute
tiles.scene: A student carries a cloth lunch bag while riding a local battery-run easy bike under strong midday sun.

tiles.label: Hot Bag
tiles.scene: The student's lunch bag rests in a hot classroom corner beside a still ceiling fan, long before lunch.

tiles.label: Sour Smell
tiles.scene: At lunchtime the student opens the tiffin box, notices an unpleasant smell, and pulls back without eating.

tiles.label: Uneaten Lunch
tiles.scene: At the end of lunch break, a full steel tiffin sits untouched beside a hungry student in a Rajshahi classroom.

tiles.label: Extra Purchase
tiles.scene: The hungry student buys a replacement lunch from a modest Rajshahi campus-area food stall.

questions: Which two scenes show what the heat costs the student?
When has packed food become unappealing before you could eat it?
Is food waste or the extra lunch expense the bigger problem?
Why might a lunch bag become hot before noon?
If a student skips the spoiled meal, what problem follows?
What could you try in 7 days for at most 1,500 BDT? Who might pay if it worked?

seed_funding.pilot: Ask ten students or workers how they carry lunch, how long it stays warm, and how often food must be discarded; use a food thermometer if available.
seed_funding.potential_customer: Students, workers, households, or food sellers
seed_funding.test_metric: Time without cooling, discarded meals, and replacement-lunch costs
seed_funding.note: Optional cash ceiling for a first experiment, not money required to begin or a full launch budget. Start with tools and relationships already available; pay partners fairly and account for founder time before scaling.

evidence.editor_note: The sources establish food-safety risk in high heat and Rajshahi heat conditions. The tiffin story is an illustrative student scenario; it does not diagnose spoilage from smell alone.

tiles.scene: The farmer shows an opened seed packet to the seller, who cannot identify its batch.

tiles.label: Missing Batch
tiles.scene: A farmer searches an opened seed packet for a usable batch mark but finds none legible.

questions: Which two scenes give a farmer evidence of a problem?
How do farmers near you choose seed sellers?
Is missing batch information or weak sprouts more serious?
Why is poor germination costly even if seeds are cheap?
If seeds fail after planting, what evidence could a farmer still gather?
What could you try in 14 days for at most 5,000 BDT? Who might pay if it worked?

seed_funding.pilot: Ask growers what proof they receive and run small labeled germination checks on purchased samples.
seed_funding.test_metric: Missing seed records, germination results, and farmer losses
seed_funding.note: Optional cash ceiling for a first experiment, not money required to begin or a full launch budget. Start with tools and relationships already available; pay partners fairly and account for founder time before scaling.

evidence.editor_note: The 2024 faulty-seed case is outside Rajshahi; the card asks about a small farmer's general purchasing risk, not local misconduct.

cards.title: UNCLEAR REPAIR TERMS
cards.focus: A phone owner cannot easily know the final repair cost, part quality, or pickup date before leaving a device.

tiles.label: Cracked Screen
tiles.scene: A student shows a cracked Android phone screen at a local repair counter.

tiles.label: Two Parts
tiles.scene: A technician shows a lower-cost and a higher-cost replacement screen in separate trays.

tiles.label: Vague Price
tiles.scene: A technician gestures about possible costs while the phone owner holds cash and has no written quote.

tiles.label: Unlabeled Parts
tiles.scene: Two replacement screens with no clear quality labels lie beside an opened phone.

tiles.label: Delayed Pickup
tiles.scene: A customer arrives for the phone, but it remains disassembled on the workbench.

tiles.label: Repeat Fault
tiles.scene: A newly repaired phone screen flickers again while the owner looks disappointed.

questions: Which two scenes could lead to a repair dispute?
What would you ask before leaving your phone for repair?
Is an unclear cost or unknown part quality more worrying?
Why can a verbal quote change after a device is opened?
If a repair fails soon after pickup, who bears the cost?
What could you try in 7 days for at most 1,500 BDT? Who might pay if it worked?

seed_funding.pilot: Observe twenty repair quotes at a willing shop and ask customers which terms were unclear.
seed_funding.test_metric: Unclear quotes, repair delays, repeat faults, and disputes
seed_funding.note: Optional cash ceiling for a first experiment, not money required to begin or a full launch budget. Start with tools and relationships already available; pay partners fairly and account for founder time before scaling.

evidence.editor_note: The source describes a transparent repair model; the card tests whether a simpler local version would help.

cards.title: LPG OVERCHARGING
cards.focus: A household may face a cooking-gas price or delivery fee that differs from what it expected.

tiles.label: Empty Cylinder
tiles.scene: A home cook finds that the kitchen LPG cylinder is empty before preparing a meal.

tiles.label: Shop Quote
tiles.scene: A customer asks the price at a neighborhood cylinder shop.

tiles.label: Old Price Notice
tiles.scene: A faded LPG price notice hangs behind a seller who quotes a different price; numbers unreadable.

tiles.label: Delivery Fee
tiles.scene: A delivery worker brings a cylinder to a flat and points to a separate fee on a receipt.

tiles.label: No Receipt
tiles.scene: A customer hands over cash for an LPG cylinder but receives no itemized receipt.

tiles.label: Carrying Cylinder
tiles.scene: A household member carries an empty cylinder toward another shop after hearing a high quote.

questions: Which two scenes show what the customer actually pays?
How do households near you learn the current cylinder price?
Is a hidden delivery fee or an old price notice more misleading?
Why can a delivery price differ from a headline price?
If buyers compare shops while out of gas, what cost appears?
What could you try in 7 days for at most 1,500 BDT? Who might pay if it worked?

seed_funding.pilot: Compare a current official price with quotes and receipts at several local shops.
seed_funding.test_metric: Difference between official, quoted, and paid cylinder prices
seed_funding.note: Optional cash ceiling for a first experiment, not money required to begin or a full launch budget. Start with tools and relationships already available; pay partners fairly and account for founder time before scaling.

evidence.editor_note: Do not claim underweight cylinders; the documented issue is price variation and overcharging.

cards.title: LOST BAKI RECORDS
cards.focus: A neighborhood shop and customer can disagree when informal credit records are missing or unclear.

tiles.label: Credit Sale
tiles.scene: A grocer hands everyday items to a familiar customer who will pay later.

tiles.label: Paper Khata
tiles.scene: The shopkeeper writes the amount in a worn Bengali account notebook.

tiles.label: Missing Page
tiles.scene: The shopkeeper searches a damaged ledger page for an old entry.

tiles.label: Customer Memory
tiles.scene: Customer and shopkeeper disagree politely over the amount owed.

tiles.label: Faded Ink
tiles.scene: A shopkeeper tries to read an old baki entry whose ink has faded in the paper khata.

tiles.label: Unpaid Month
tiles.scene: A shopkeeper counts little cash beside several unpaid baki entries at month end.

questions: Which two scenes make a baki dispute more likely?
Where have you seen a shop keep a paper khata?
Is a missing page or a remembered amount stronger evidence?
Why might shops still prefer informal credit?
If a customer disputes a baki total, what happens to trust?
What could you try in 7 days for at most 1,500 BDT? Who might pay if it worked?

seed_funding.pilot: Observe one willing shop for a week and note how baki sales, payments, and disputes are recorded.
seed_funding.test_metric: Disputed balances, missing entries, and time spent checking the khata
seed_funding.note: Optional cash ceiling for a first experiment, not money required to begin or a full launch budget. Start with tools and relationships already available; pay partners fairly and account for founder time before scaling.

evidence.editor_note: Existing Bangladeshi products confirm this is an active market; students should test a distinct service hypothesis rather than assume there is no competition.

cards.title: APPLICATION MISTAKES
cards.focus: A student can miss an application deadline because a photo, scan, or document is wrong or missing.

tiles.label: Document Pile
tiles.scene: An applicant sorts certificates, photo prints, and ID photocopies on a table.

tiles.label: Photo Size
tiles.scene: A print-shop worker checks a passport-style photo against an application size guide.

tiles.label: Scan Quality
tiles.scene: A student notices that a phone scan has cut off one certificate corner.

tiles.label: Deadline Clock
tiles.scene: The applicant checks a deadline on a phone while waiting to print.

tiles.label: Rejected Photo
tiles.scene: An applicant sees a photo upload rejected because its size is wrong; no readable text.

tiles.label: Exposed Copies
tiles.scene: Unclaimed identity photocopies lie on a public print-shop counter with details illegible.

questions: Which two scenes could make an application incomplete?
What paperwork has taken you more than one visit?
Is a bad scan or the wrong photo harder to notice?
Why do different applications need different formats?
If a deadline is missed, what chance is lost?
What could you try in 7 days for at most 1,500 BDT? Who might pay if it worked?

seed_funding.pilot: Ask ten applicants to walk through one real checklist using their own documents; retain no copies.
seed_funding.test_metric: Missing documents, rejected scans, and time lost before deadlines
seed_funding.note: Optional cash ceiling for a first experiment, not money required to begin or a full launch budget. Start with tools and relationships already available; pay partners fairly and account for founder time before scaling.

evidence.editor_note: The prospectus is one example of detailed document requirements, not a Rajshahi job posting.

cards.title: HARD-TO-FIND MEDICINE
cards.focus: A person with a prescription may need to visit several pharmacies to find the exact medicine and strength.

tiles.label: Prescription
tiles.scene: A patient holds a prescription with no readable medical details at a pharmacy counter.

tiles.label: Empty Shelf
tiles.scene: A pharmacist checks an empty space where a requested medicine would normally be stored.

tiles.label: Second Shop
tiles.scene: The patient walks to another licensed pharmacy with the prescription.

tiles.label: No Stock Answer
tiles.scene: A pharmacist tries to call another shop about stock, but the phone goes unanswered while the patient waits.

tiles.label: Wrong Strength
tiles.scene: A patient compares two medicine packs of different strengths while a pharmacist checks the prescription; all text illegible.

tiles.label: Long Search
tiles.scene: A patient carrying a prescription passes several pharmacy counters without finding the required pack.

questions: Which two scenes cause unnecessary travel?
How do people usually find a medicine that one shop lacks?
Is an empty shelf or the wrong strength a bigger problem?
Why must a pharmacist confirm the exact medicine and strength?
What could go wrong if a patient buys a different pack without advice?
What could you try in 14 days for at most 3,000 BDT? Who might pay if it worked?

seed_funding.pilot: Ask ten consenting patients and licensed pharmacies which stock questions cause wasted trips; do not handle prescriptions.
seed_funding.test_metric: Unnecessary pharmacy trips and uncertainty about exact stock
seed_funding.note: Optional cash ceiling for a first experiment, not money required to begin or a full launch budget. Start with tools and relationships already available; pay partners fairly and account for founder time before scaling.

evidence.editor_note: National supply disruption and an existing pharmacy-stock product ground the need and possible model, not measured demand in Rajshahi. No medicine substitution or diagnosis should be suggested.

cards.title: COSTLY FARM MACHINES
cards.focus: A small Barind-area farmer needs a machine briefly but cannot justify buying it alone.

tiles.label: Small Plot
tiles.scene: A farmer stands beside a modest Barind crop plot that needs preparation.

tiles.label: Costly Machine
tiles.scene: The farmer examines a powered farm tool at a dealer but hesitates at its price tag.

tiles.label: No Available Tool
tiles.scene: A farmer reaches an empty machinery shed during the busy season.

tiles.label: Clashing Needs

tiles.label: Unfamiliar Controls
tiles.scene: A farmer hesitates at the controls of a large farm machine without an operator nearby.

tiles.label: Machine Breakdown
tiles.scene: A mechanic repairs a stalled rented farm machine while the next farmer waits beside a ready field.

questions: Which two scenes could delay a farmer at the busiest time?
What farm tool would be useful to hire only occasionally?
Is an unavailable tool or a broken one harder during planting?
Why does timing matter more during planting or harvest?
If one machine serves several farms, who waits?
What could you try in 14 days for at most 5,000 BDT? Who might pay if it worked?

seed_funding.pilot: Ask growers and equipment owners when machines are unavailable, idle, or too costly to hire.
seed_funding.test_metric: Unmet machine demand, idle equipment, and hire costs
seed_funding.note: Optional cash ceiling for a first experiment, not money required to begin or a full launch budget. Start with tools and relationships already available; pay partners fairly and account for founder time before scaling.

evidence.editor_note: Existing machinery services show this is an established model; test availability and trust in one local context.

cards.title: ELDER ISOLATION
cards.focus: An older resident may want dependable contact or practical help while keeping control over visits and private information.

tiles.label: Quiet Home
tiles.scene: An older person sits alone beside a phone in a modest Rajshahi home.

tiles.label: Missed Call
tiles.scene: The phone shows an unanswered call icon while the person is outside in the courtyard.

tiles.label: Unanswered Gate
tiles.scene: A known neighbor calls from an older resident’s gate but receives no answer.

tiles.label: Heavy Errand
tiles.scene: An older resident carries a heavy grocery bag home alone along a Rajshahi lane.

tiles.label: Busy Contact
tiles.scene: A chosen contact sees a missed call while occupied at work and cannot answer immediately.

tiles.label: Unwanted Knock
tiles.scene: An older resident hesitates when an unfamiliar visitor knocks at the home gate.

questions: Which two scenes show why contact can be difficult?
When might an older resident want contact or practical help?
Is a missed call or an unwanted visit more troubling?
Why might a chosen contact be hard to reach?
What could happen if helpers ignore an older person’s preferences?
What could you try in 14 days for at most 5,000 BDT? Who might pay if it worked?

seed_funding.pilot: Ask willing older residents what contact they want, what they decline, and which practical gaps remain.
seed_funding.test_metric: Desired contact, missed help, and privacy preferences
seed_funding.note: Optional cash ceiling for a first experiment, not money required to begin or a full launch budget. Start with tools and relationships already available; pay partners fairly and account for founder time before scaling.

evidence.editor_note: The card avoids assuming every older adult has relatives, a smartphone, or a desire for visits.
